title: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop
gist: In an Ars Live discussion, RUSI's Joseph Jarnecki argued that public cloud data centers have become legitimate military targets because militaries use them (dual use), and that cheap drones impose 100x-plus economic damage relative to munition cost. After Amazon facilities in the Middle East were attacked in the 2026 Iran war and Russia/Ukraine traded data-center strikes, he expects such attacks to continue.

insights.claim: Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time in the Middle East in 2026, while Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other's data centers.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Physical war risk is now a live factor for hyperscaler capex siting, insurance and regional cloud availability.
insights.locator: Amazon data centers came under military attack

insights.claim: Joseph Jarnecki of RUSI argues that militaries' use of public and private cloud compute for battlefield management, HR and resource management can turn civilian data centers into military objects that adversaries have an incentive to target.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler defense contracts carry a hidden cost: they may raise the physical targeting risk of commercial regions.
insights.quote: Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object
insights.locator: We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use

insights.claim: Jarnecki estimates, very conservatively, that the investment by AWS and others in Gulf data centers exceeds the cost of the Iranian Shahed drones used to attack them by 100x or more, making data centers lucrative targets for imposing economic cost.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Extreme cost asymmetry means deterrence-by-defense is hard; expect rising spend on physical protection and geographic diversification.
insights.quote: I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more
insights.locator: The second reason that we’ve seen targeting

insights.claim: Russia's largest public cloud data centers such as Yandex, along with American hyperscalers based in the Gulf, have been targeted to impose economic costs that would be hard to impose otherwise.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Cloud providers in conflict-adjacent regions face war-risk discounting of their regional assets.
insights.quote: So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption.
insights.locator: The second reason that we’ve seen targeting

insights.claim: Ukraine anticipated Russian targeting of civilian digital infrastructure and conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the February 2022 full-scale invasion.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Ukraine's playbook supports demand for sovereign-cloud-abroad and cross-border failover services from hyperscalers.
insights.locator: I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set

insights.claim: Jarnecki expects military targeting of data centers to continue beyond 2026 because they are relatively squishy, easy to find, and complex enough to induce cascading risks when hit by kinetic munitions.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Price in persistent geopolitical risk for data center REITs and hyperscaler regions in or near conflict zones.
insights.quote: data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find

insights.claim: Hardening or building data centers underground, and using orbital data centers or LEO constellations such as Starlink as backups, were discussed as options to withstand physical attacks on cloud infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Physical-security threats may create incremental demand for hardened facilities and space-based backup capacity.
